**Hero image:** a paper-craft corner of a living room in morning light — a mat, a kettlebell, a low step, a band on a door handle, a laptop on a stool showing a countdown — under the title. https://www.collegica.org/static/img/aging-well/exercise-sessions-hero.jpg

[Planning to Age Well, with AI](/aging-well/ai-planning.md) makes an argument
that is easy to agree with and hard to act on: muscle is one of three kinds
of capital, it compounds when you train it and decays when you do not, and
the plan for it is about three hours a week. The article gives the skeleton
— two full-body sessions, a squat, a hinge, a push, a pull, a carry,
something fast once a week, balance most days — and then, honestly, leaves
you at the door of a gym with a prompt to paste into a chatbot.

This article is what happens after the door. It is about **routines**: the
families of movement worth building a session from, why the order and the
rests matter as much as the exercises, and how thirty minutes that you
actually do beats sixty that you plan. Then it introduces
[**OWL Sessions**](https://www.collegica.org/sessions/), a small app that turns those routines into a
timed session on your own screen — each move shown by a demonstrator, a
countdown, a rep count, and one minute of rest in the places a body needs
it. It runs entirely in the page. Nothing is uploaded, no account exists.

> **TL;DR**
>
>
> 1. **Three families, one session.** Anti-movement core work (dead bug,
>    bird dog, planks, the Pallof press), loaded movement with one hand or
>    two (squat, hinge, swing, press, row, carry), and aerobic minutes on
>    your feet (marching, jogging, step-ups, skater hops). A session takes a
>    few from each, in that order, with a mobility move to open and close.
> 2. **The rest is part of the routine.** One minute between blocks, not
>    between exercises. Enough to reset the breath and the form; not enough
>    to check the phone.
> 3. **Thirty, forty-five or sixty minutes.** The same five blocks, scaled.
>    The thirty is the one to protect; the others are the same session with
>    more rounds.
> 4. **The app runs it.** [OWL Sessions](https://www.collegica.org/sessions/) plays a ten-second clip
>    of each move on a loop under a timer and a rep count, beeps at the
>    turns, rests you between blocks, and never leaves the page.
> 5. **The clips are generated and checked, not filmed and certified.** A
>    person compared every one against the exercise; a trainer has not. The
>    app says so in its footer, and this article says so here.
> 6. **Stop when form goes, not when the timer says.** The timer is there to
>    remove decisions, not to overrule your back.

## Why routines, not exercises

The muscle plan fails in a specific way. Not for lack of knowledge — the
squat, the hinge and the carry are not secrets — but because each session
asks for a dozen small decisions before it starts: which moves, how many,
in what order, for how long, how much rest. Every decision is a place to
stop. A routine is a session in which those decisions were made once,
earlier, by a calmer version of you, and the only decision left is whether
to press Start.

Three properties make a routine one you can keep:

- **It is short enough on the worst day.** Thirty minutes including the
  warm-up and the rests. The longer versions exist for better days; they
  are not the default.
- **It needs almost nothing.** A mat, one kettlebell or a heavy bag, a
  band, and a stair. Every move in the library below has a version with
  no weight at all.
- **It is the same shape every time.** Five blocks in the same order, so
  the body knows what is coming and the mind stops negotiating.

## The three families

The [earlier article](/aging-well/ai-planning.md#plan-two-the-muscles) named
the movements by what they do to a barbell: squat, hinge, push, pull,
carry. That is the right list for a gym. For a living-room routine that
also has to protect a back and a pair of hips into the eighties, it helps
to group by what the trunk is doing.

### Anti-movement: the trunk holds still

The family that dead bug and bird dog belong to. The limbs move, or a load
pulls, and the job is to let nothing else happen. This is the foundation
under every lift and every recovery from a stumble, and it is the family
most people skip because it does not feel like exercise.

| The trunk resists | Moves, easiest first |
|---|---|
| **Extension** (the spine wants to arch) | Dead bug; front plank; stir the pot on a ball; ab-wheel rollout from the knees; hollow hold |
| **Rotation** (a load tries to twist you) | Bird dog; Pallof press with a band; suitcase carry; renegade row; half-kneeling chop |
| **Side bending** | Side plank from the knees, then the feet; suitcase carry again; Copenhagen plank |

Stuart McGill's *Big Three* — a curl-up with the hands under the low back,
the side plank, the bird dog — is the set most often prescribed for a sore
back, held for short counts, several sets, daily. Two of the three are in
the library. The curl-up is not, for a reason explained below.

### Loaded: one hand or two

Where the strength is built. Two hands first, because the load is easier
to control; one hand next, because carrying a suitcase, opening a door
against wind and catching yourself on a rail are all one-handed.

| | Two hands | One hand |
|---|---|---|
| **Squat** | Goblet squat | — |
| **Hinge** | Kettlebell deadlift; kettlebell swing, the power move | Single-leg deadlift, later |
| **Push** | Floor press | Half-kneeling overhead press |
| **Pull** | Two-dumbbell row | Single-arm row, hand on a bench |
| **Carry** | Front-loaded carry | Suitcase carry |

The swing is the one the earlier article asked for and most routines
leave out: something fast and light, once a week, because power falls
faster than strength and power is what turns a trip into a step.

### On your feet: the aerobic minutes

Not a run. Minutes on the feet that raise the breath, keep the balance
honest and can be done in socks beside the mat: marching in place with
the knees to hip height, jogging in place, step-ups on the bottom stair,
skater hops from one foot to the other, and a brisk walk on the days the
session does not happen. The WHO's figure for adults is 150 to 300 minutes
of moderate aerobic activity a week; two sessions plus most-day walks get
there.

### Opening and closing

The cat-camel — slow rounding and sinking of the spine on hands and knees
— is the move every session should start and end with. It is a warm-up
for the joints, not a stretch, and it is the one exercise in the library
with no wrong side.

## How a session is built

Five blocks, always in this order, one minute of rest between each:

| Block | Why here | In the 30-minute session |
|---|---|---|
| **Warm-up** | Joints first, then the pulse | Cat-camel, march, jog — 3 min |
| **Core** | Fresh, before the load | Dead bug, bird dog, side and front plank, glute bridge, Pallof press — 9 min |
| **Strength** | The reason for the session | Goblet squat, deadlift, swing, press, row — 6½ min |
| **Aerobic** | Breath up while form still holds | Jog, step-ups, skater hops — 5 min |
| **Cool-down** | Back to resting | Cat-camel, march, glute bridge — 2½ min |

The forty-five and sixty-minute sessions are the same five blocks with
more rounds and one or two more moves per block; they do not add new
families. The one minute between blocks is deliberate. Rest between
individual exercises invites the phone; rest between blocks is long
enough to reset the breath and short enough to keep the session's shape.
Within a block, the moves alternate the muscles they load, which is the
rest.

Two rules the timer cannot enforce. **Stop a set when form goes**, not
when the countdown says; the rep count on the screen is a ceiling, not a
target. And **progress by making the move harder before making it
longer**: a lower knee on the side plank becomes a straight leg, a bare
squat gets a kettlebell, a march becomes a jog. The sessions do not get
longer; the moves get heavier.

## OWL Sessions

[OWL Sessions](https://www.collegica.org/sessions/) is the routine above, run for you. It sits
beside [OWL Planner](https://www.collegica.org/owl/), the money tool of the same framework, and
follows the same rules: a browser tab, your own machine, nothing sent
anywhere.

Pick a length and press Start. The app walks the five blocks. For each
move it plays a ten-second clip of a demonstrator on a loop, shows the
family, the name and one coaching cue, and counts down the working time.
For moves with a tempo it derives a rep count; for holds and the aerobic
minutes it shows the seconds left. A short tone marks each turn and the
last three seconds. Between blocks the screen turns green for the minute
of rest and names what comes next. A bar along the bottom shows the whole
session and where you are in it. Pause, skip and stop do what they say,
and any move can be previewed without starting a session.

The library has seventeen moves, one clip each:

| Family | Moves |
|---|---|
| Anti-extension | Dead bug, front plank |
| Anti-rotation | Bird dog, Pallof press |
| Anti-lateral-flexion | Side plank |
| Hip hinge | Glute bridge |
| Mobility | Cat-camel |
| Weights, two hands | Goblet squat, kettlebell deadlift, kettlebell swing |
| Weights, one hand | Suitcase carry, single-arm row, half-kneeling press |
| Aerobic and balance | Marching in place, jogging in place, step-ups, skater hops |

The plans are three short files anyone can read, and each adds up exactly
to its length including the rests. Changing a session is editing a list.

## How the clips were made, and what that means

The demonstrator is not a person who was filmed. Each clip was generated
from a written description of the exercise — the starting position, the
movement, the position of the limbs that must not move, the camera — by
a video model, through the same route this site uses for its images. That
choice deserves a plain account.

**Why generated.** Filming seventeen exercises well needs a studio, a
demonstrator whose form a trainer has checked, and a day. Generating
them cost under thirty dollars of credits and an afternoon, and it made
the library possible before the app had earned a film day.

**What went wrong, and was caught.** Five models were given the dead bug
first. The cheapest produced the only correct one; three of the others
performed a different or easier exercise, cleanly and convincingly: feet
on the floor instead of in tabletop, a leg raise instead of a dead bug.
That is the failure mode to understand about generated exercise video.
It does not look sloppy. It looks like a competent person doing a
slightly different exercise, and someone who does not know the move
would never notice. So every clip in the library was compared, frame by
sampled frame, against the exercise it claims to show. Two standing
moves and the step-ups came back with the head cropped from one model and
were remade with another. The McGill curl-up came back as a crunch twice,
however explicitly the description said otherwise, and was left out
rather than shipped wrong.

**What the check was, and was not.** An editor with the exercise in
front of them, not a trainer. The clips show the movement; they are not a
standard of form to imitate exactly, and the app says so under every
session. If you teach these moves and see something wrong in one, the
[research folder](/aging-well/research/exercise-sessions.md)
has every contact sheet and the note that goes with it.

**What it cost.** Twenty-nine generations for seventeen clips, about
five hundred credits; the comparison of the five models is written up
with its prices. The prompts, the job ids and the sheets are all in the
folder, so the library can be regenerated or extended by anyone with the
same tools.

## What to do this week

- **Do the thirty-minute session twice.** Not the sixty. Note which move
  you skipped and why; that is next week's adjustment.
- **Measure the two markers the earlier article asked for** before the
  first session: grip strength if you have a dynamometer, and five
  sit-to-stands, timed. The routine is for moving those.
- **Set up the room once.** Mat rolled out, one weight, a band on the
  door, the bottom stair clear. The session should cost no setup.
- **Walk on the other days.** The aerobic block is a floor, not the
  plan.
- **Tell a trainer which clip looks wrong.** The library improves the way
  everything on this site does: one correction at a time, with the
  evidence beside it.

## Sources

Research notes — the movement families, the session structure, the
five-model comparison, and every clip's contact sheet — are in [the
accompanying folder](/aging-well/research/exercise-sessions.md);
the app's source is in [`apps/owl-sessions`](/apps/owl-sessions.md)
and [`website/static/js/sessions`](https://github.com/Collegica/collegica/tree/main/website/static/js/sessions).

- **The framework.** [Planning to Age Well, with AI](/aging-well/ai-planning.md),
  plan two, and its sources.
- **Activity guidelines.** World Health Organization, [Guidelines on
  physical activity and sedentary behaviour](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240015128),
  25 November 2020: 150–300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity a week
  for adults, muscle-strengthening on two or more days, and for adults 65
  and over multicomponent balance and strength training on three or more
  days.
- **The Big Three.** Stuart McGill, *Back Mechanic* (Backfitpro, 2015),
  for the curl-up, side plank and bird dog as a daily set.
- **The clips.** The [five-model comparison](/aging-well/research/exercise-clips.md)
  and the [library notes](/apps/owl-sessions.md),
  with the prompt template from the site's `exercise-videos` skill.
